title: Weather, seasons and plans: the future with 'бу́ду'
objectives: I can say what the weather is like with 'те́пло', 'хо́лодно', 'Іде́ дощ.', 'Іде́ сніг.' and 'Сві́тить со́нце.', and ask 'Яка́ сього́дні пого́да?'.
I can name the days of the week and say on which day something happens with 'у' or 'в' and the accusative.
I can say in which season something happens with 'взи́мку', 'навесні́', 'влі́тку' and 'восени́'.
I can talk about plans with the future 'бу́ду' plus an infinitive, and say where I will be with 'бу́ду' alone.
I can invite a friend, accept or decline, and explain how 'п’я́тниця', 'дощ' and 'вихідні́' are pronounced and how the stress tells 'те́пло' from 'тепло́'.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'понеді́лка': the 'о' of the last syllable drops out in the other forms, as in 'ри́нок', 'ри́нку'. It is the day after 'неді́ля', Sunday. Like every day of the week, it is written with a small letter.

example.source: I work on Monday.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'вівто́рка'. The first 'в' is [ʋ] before a vowel and the second is [w] before 'т'. It always takes 'у', even after a vowel: 'у вівто́рок'.

example.source: Taras is at home on Tuesday.

vocabulary.note: The accusative moves the stress: 'у сере́ду', on Wednesday. Genitive 'середи́'.

example.target: У сере́ду я чита́ю в бібліоте́ці.
example.source: On Wednesday I read in the library.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'четверга́': the other forms add 'г' and put the stress on the ending. The accusative is the same as the nominative: 'у четве́р'.

example.source: It will rain on Thursday.

vocabulary.note: The fifth day of the week, from the same root as 'п’ять', five. The accusative is 'п’я́тницю': 'у п’я́тницю'.

example.target: У п’я́тницю ми обі́даємо в кафе́.
example.source: On Friday we have lunch at the café.

vocabulary.note: The accusative is 'субо́ту': 'у субо́ту', or 'в субо́ту' after a vowel.

example.source: What are you doing on Saturday?

vocabulary.note: The 'д' is soft before 'і' and the 'л' is soft before 'я'. The accusative is 'неді́лю': 'у неді́лю'.

example.source: I don't work on Sunday.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ти́жня': in the other forms both the 'е' and the 'д' drop out. The final 'нь' is soft.

example.source: This week will be very interesting.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: plural noun, declined like an adjective
vocabulary.note: The plural of 'вихідни́й', a day off, a noun that began as the adjective in 'вихідни́й день' and so keeps adjective endings. It takes plural words: 'мої́ вихідні́'. 'На вихідни́х', on the weekend, uses its locative plural, met whole here; the plural cases come in A2.

example.source: I relax on the weekend.

vocabulary.note: The 'г' is the voiced [ɦ]. 'Пого́да га́рна.' says the weather is nice.

example.source: What is the weather like today?

vocabulary.note: 'Сві́тить со́нце.', the sun is shining, uses the verb 'сві́тити', to shine.

example.source: The sun is shining today.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'дощу́', with the stress on the ending. Rain 'goes': 'Іде́ дощ.', it is raining; after a vowel the form is 'йде': 'Сього́дні йде дощ.'

example.source: It is raining now.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'сні́гу'. The final 'г' stays a voiced [ɦ]. Snow 'goes' as rain does: 'Іде́ сніг.', it is snowing.

example.source: It often snows in Canada.

vocabulary.note: It is the whole predicate of a sentence with no subject, and never changes. With the stress on the end, 'тепло́' is a different word, the neuter noun for warmth.

example.source: It is warm today.

vocabulary.note: Like 'те́пло', it is the predicate of a sentence with no subject and never changes: 'Там ду́же хо́лодно.', it is very cold there.

example.source: It is very cold there in winter.

vocabulary.note: 'In spring' is the adverb 'навесні́'. The accusative is 'весну́', with the stress still on the end.

example.source: Spring in Kyiv is very beautiful.

vocabulary.note: 'In summer' is the adverb 'влі́тку', or 'улі́тку' after a consonant and at the start of a sentence.

example.source: I love summer very much.

vocabulary.note: Future 'бу́ду', 'бу́деш', 'бу́де', 'бу́демо', 'бу́дете', 'бу́дуть'. Its one present form is 'є', which states existence and possession; otherwise the present has no verb.

example.source: Tomorrow I will be at the university.

vocabulary.note: Regular, like 'чита́ти': 'відпочива́ю', 'відпочива́єш'. The 'д' stays a voiced [d] before 'п'.

example.source: On Sunday we will relax.

vocabulary.note: It asks for a time: a day, a season or an hour.

example.source: When will you be at home?

dialogues.title: The weekend forecast
dialogues.context: On a Thursday, Oksana and Sam are at Andrii's café, reading the weather forecast for the weekend on Oksana's phone. The two friends say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, яка́ пого́да бу́де на вихідни́х?
lines.source: Oksana, what will the weather be like on the weekend?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, which weather will-be on days-off?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: У субо́ту бу́де те́пло.
lines.source: On Saturday it will be warm.
lines.source_literal: On Saturday will-be warm.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А в неді́лю?
lines.source: And on Sunday?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: У неді́лю бу́де хо́лодно. І бу́де дощ.
lines.source: On Sunday it will be cold. And it will rain.
lines.source_literal: On Sunday will-be cold. And will-be rain.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Що ти бу́деш роби́ти в субо́ту?
lines.source: What will you do on Saturday?
lines.source_literal: What you will-be to-do on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Я бу́ду працюва́ти вра́нці, а по́тім бу́ду відпочива́ти в па́рку.
lines.source: I'll work in the morning, and then I'll relax in the park.
lines.source_literal: I will-be to-work in-morning, and then will-be to-rest in park.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Я ду́же люблю́ парк восени́.
lines.source: I really love the park in autumn.
lines.source_literal: I very love park in-autumn.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Хо́чеш у парк у субо́ту? О тре́тій.
lines.source: Do you want to go to the park on Saturday? At three.
lines.source_literal: You-want to park on Saturday? At third.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, до́бре! А в неді́лю я бу́ду вдо́ма.
lines.source: Yes, OK! And on Sunday I'll be at home.
lines.source_literal: Yes, well! And on Sunday I will-be at-home.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Чому́?
lines.source: Why?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Тому́ що в неді́лю бу́де дощ!
lines.source: Because it will rain on Sunday!
lines.source_literal: Because on Sunday will-be rain!

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Розумі́ю. До субо́ти!
lines.source: I see. See you on Saturday!
lines.source_literal: I-understand. Until Saturday!

dialogues.title: Saturday or Sunday?
dialogues.context: Taras phones his sister Olena, a doctor, to invite her to the park. Brother and sister say 'ти' to each other.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Приві́т, Оле́но! Хо́чеш у парк у субо́ту?
lines.source: Hi, Olena! Do you want to go to the park on Saturday?
lines.source_literal: Hi, Olena! You-want to park on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: У субо́ту? А яка́ бу́де пого́да?
lines.source: On Saturday? And what will the weather be like?
lines.source_literal: On Saturday? And which will-be weather?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Сього́дні хо́лодно, а в субо́ту бу́де те́пло.
lines.source: It's cold today, but on Saturday it will be warm.
lines.source_literal: Today cold, and on Saturday will-be warm.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Ні, Тара́се, у субо́ту я працю́ю.
lines.source: No, Taras, I'm working on Saturday.
lines.source_literal: No, Taras, on Saturday I work.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: А коли́ ти бу́деш удо́ма?
lines.source: So when will you be at home?
lines.source_literal: And when you will-be at-home?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: У неді́лю я не працю́ю. Хо́чеш у парк у неді́лю?
lines.source: I'm not working on Sunday. Do you want to go to the park on Sunday?
lines.source_literal: On Sunday I not work. You-want to park on Sunday?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Але́ в неді́лю бу́де дощ!
lines.source: But it will rain on Sunday!
lines.source_literal: But on Sunday will-be rain!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Мо́жна сиді́ти в кафе́. Там те́пло, і є смачна́ ка́ва.
lines.source: We can sit in the café. It's warm there, and there's good coffee.
lines.source_literal: Possible to-sit in café. There warm, and is tasty coffee.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре! О котрі́й?
lines.source: OK! What time?
lines.source_literal: Well! At which?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Об одина́дцятій.
lines.source: At eleven.
lines.source_literal: At eleventh.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́бре. До неді́лі!
lines.source: OK. See you on Sunday!
lines.source_literal: Well. Until Sunday!

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Бува́й!
lines.source: Bye!

dialogues.title: Winter in Canada, autumn in Kyiv
dialogues.context: In class, Iryna Petrivna asks Sam about the seasons in Canada and tells him about Kyiv. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Се́ме, яка́ пого́да в Кана́ді взи́мку?
lines.source: Sam, what is the weather like in Canada in winter?
lines.source_literal: Sam, which weather in Canada in-winter?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У Кана́ді взи́мку ду́же хо́лодно. Ча́сто йде сніг.
lines.source: In Canada it's very cold in winter. It often snows.
lines.source_literal: In Canada in-winter very cold. Often goes snow.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: У Ки́єві взи́мку хо́лодно, але́ не ду́же.
lines.source: In Kyiv it's cold in winter, but not very.
lines.source_literal: In Kyiv in-winter cold, but not very.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: А сніг у Ки́єві є?
lines.source: And is there snow in Kyiv?
lines.source_literal: And snow in Kyiv is?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, є, але́ не завжди́. А яке́ лі́то в Кана́ді?
lines.source: Yes, there is, but not always. And what is summer like in Canada?
lines.source_literal: Yes, is, but not always. And which summer in Canada?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: У Кана́ді влі́тку те́пло. Ми відпочива́ємо на о́зері.
lines.source: In Canada it's warm in summer. We relax at the lake.
lines.source_literal: In Canada in-summer warm. We rest on lake.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А навесні́?
lines.source: And in spring?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Навесні́ споча́тку хо́лодно, а по́тім те́пло.
lines.source: In spring it's cold at first, and then it's warm.
lines.source_literal: In-spring at-first cold, and then warm.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А ви лю́бите зи́му?
lines.source: And do you like winter?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, ду́же. Я люблю́ сніг.
lines.source: Yes, very much. I love snow.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: А я люблю́ о́сінь. Восени́ Ки́їв ду́же га́рний.
lines.source: And I love autumn. Kyiv is very beautiful in autumn.
lines.source_literal: And I love autumn. In-autumn Kyiv very beautiful.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Так, але́ восени́ тут ча́сто йде дощ!
lines.source: Yes, but it often rains here in autumn!
lines.source_literal: Yes, but in-autumn here often goes rain!

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Ви бу́дете в Кана́ді взи́мку?
lines.source: Will you be in Canada in winter?
lines.source_literal: You will-be in Canada in-winter?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ні, я бу́ду тут, у Ки́єві. Тут бу́де сніг!
lines.source: No, I'll be here, in Kyiv. There will be snow here!
lines.source_literal: No, I will-be here, in Kyiv. Here will-be snow!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: п’я́тниця, дощ, те́пло and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
The new words in this unit are read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress, and one point about voicing, under 'відпочива́ти' below, adds to them. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

The apostrophe in 'п’я́тниця' [ˈpjɑtnɪt͡sʲɑ] works as the unit on soft sounds taught. It stands after 'п' and before 'я', so the 'п' stays hard and the [j] of 'я' is sounded in full: [pj], as in English 'pure'. The word begins exactly like 'п’ять', five, because Friday is the fifth day of the week. The 'ц' at the end is soft before 'я'.

In 'дощ' [dɔʃt͡ʃ] the letter 'щ' writes two sounds, [ʃt͡ʃ], as in 'fresh cheese', and both are said in full at the end of a word, as in 'борщ'. In the genitive 'дощу́' the stress moves to the ending.

'Те́пло' and 'тепло́' are spelled with the same letters and told apart only by the stress, like 'за́мок' and 'замо́к' in the unit on stress. 'Те́пло', stressed on the first syllable, is the predicative word 'it is warm' ('Сього́дні те́пло.'). 'Тепло́', stressed on the last, is a neuter noun meaning 'warmth'. Ordinary text prints no stress mark, so the sentence decides which word is meant. The speech engines also read text without the mark, so no listening or dictation exercise asks you to hear the difference.

In 'вихідні́' [ʋɪxidʲˈnʲi] the 'д' and the 'н' are soft before 'і', while the 'х' is only slightly softened, as every consonant that cannot be fully soft is. The unstressed 'и' of the first syllable leans a little toward 'е'. The stress stays on the ending in every form: 'на вихідни́х'.

The letter 'в' keeps its two sounds:

- [ʋ] before a vowel: 'весна́', 'восени́', the first 'в' of 'вівто́рок'.
- [w] before a consonant: the second 'в' of 'вівто́рок' [ʋiwˈtɔrɔk], and 'взи́мку' [ˈwzɪmku], 'влі́тку', 'вдо́ма'.

A few more words follow rules already met:

- 'неді́ля' [nɛˈdʲilʲɑ]: the 'д' is soft before 'і' and the 'л' before 'я'.
- 'ти́ждень' [ˈtɪʒdɛnʲ]: the final 'нь' is soft, and in the genitive 'ти́жня' the 'е' and the 'д' both drop out.
- 'понеді́лок', 'вівто́рок': the 'о' of the last syllable drops out in the other forms ('понеді́лка', 'вівто́рка'), as in 'ри́нок', 'ри́нку'.
- 'сніг': the final 'г' stays the voiced [ɦ], because voiced consonants stay voiced at the end of a word.
- 'відпочива́ти': the 'д' stays a voiced [d] before the voiceless 'п'. Most Ukrainian voiced consonants keep their voice before a voiceless consonant; 'з', which the unit on stress showed partly losing its voice there, is the main exception.
- 'середа́', 'четве́р', 'восени́': the unstressed 'е' leans toward 'и'.

Stress moves in some nouns of this unit, as the unit on stress warned: 'середа́' but 'у сере́ду'; 'зима́' but 'зи́му' in the accusative; 'дощ' but 'дощу́'; 'четве́р' but 'четверга́', where the other forms also add a 'г'. Learn the stress with each form you meet.

grammar.title: The future with 'бу́ду': plans and invitations
grammar.explanation:
An imperfective verb can make its future with two words: a form of 'бу́ти', to be, followed by the infinitive of the verb. This is called the compound future, a future built from more than one word. Here 'бу́ти' is an auxiliary verb, a verb that helps to form a tense of another verb, as English 'will' does in 'I will rest'. The person is shown only by the ending of 'бу́ти'; the infinitive never changes: 'Я бу́ду відпочива́ти.', 'I will rest', literally 'I will-be to-rest'.

The forms of 'бу́ти' in the future are regular first-conjugation endings on the stem 'буд-', with the stress on the first syllable throughout. The pronoun may be left out, as in the present, because the ending shows the person: 'Бу́ду чита́ти.'

This future belongs to imperfective verbs only. As the unit on verbs explained, an imperfective verb presents an action as a process, a habit or a fact, so 'Я бу́ду чита́ти.' says that reading will go on or will happen, not that a book will be finished. A perfective verb such as 'прочита́ти' never follows 'бу́ду': perfective verbs have a future of their own, which comes in A2 together with a one-word imperfective future, 'чита́тиму', I will read. With 'іти́' and 'ї́хати' this future is uncommon for plans, because Ukrainian usually announces a trip with a perfective verb, taught in A2. At this level, say where you will be with 'бу́ти' alone: 'У субо́ту я бу́ду в па́рку.'

On its own, 'бу́ти' in the future means 'will be'. Its present has the one form 'є', which states existence and possession, and otherwise no verb at all, so the future often adds a verb where the present has none:

- 'Я вдо́ма.' 'I am at home.' against 'Я бу́ду вдо́ма.' 'I will be at home.'
- 'Сього́дні хо́лодно.' 'It is cold today.' against 'За́втра бу́де хо́лодно.' 'It will be cold tomorrow.'

A sentence about the weather with 'те́пло' or 'хо́лодно' has no subject, and then 'бу́ти' takes the form of 'він', 'вона́', 'воно́': 'бу́де'.

A fixed plan with a time word can also be in the present, as in English 'I'm working on Saturday': 'У субо́ту я працю́ю.'

Plans and invitations use these patterns:

- Asking about plans: 'Що ти бу́деш роби́ти в субо́ту?' or 'Ти бу́деш удо́ма?'
- Inviting: 'Хо́чеш у парк у субо́ту?', or 'Хо́чете...?' to someone you call 'ви'.
- Accepting: 'Так, до́бре.'
- Declining with a reason: 'Ні, у субо́ту я працю́ю.'
- Suggesting another day: 'А в неді́лю?'
- Parting until that day: 'До субо́ти!', literally 'until Saturday', with 'до' and the genitive.

In 'Хо́чеш у парк?', 'хоті́ти' is followed by a direction, 'у' plus the accusative as in the unit on going places, and needs no verb of going: literally 'you-want to park?'. 'Удо́ма' is 'вдо́ма' after a consonant, by the same rule as 'у' and 'в'.

examples.source: Do you want to go to the park on Saturday?

grammar.title: Days and seasons: saying when
grammar.explanation:
'Коли́?' asks 'when?'. This unit gives two ways to answer it: a day of the week with a preposition, and a season with an adverb. Both usually come early in the sentence, before the new information: 'У субо́ту я працю́ю.'

The days of the week are nouns, written with a small letter. Three are masculine ('понеді́лок', 'вівто́рок', 'четве́р') and four are feminine ('середа́', 'п’я́тниця', 'субо́та', 'неді́ля'). To say on which day something happens, Ukrainian uses 'у' with the accusative, the same pattern as 'Я йду в парк.', here pointing to a time instead of a place. The accusative follows the rules of the unit on food and drink:

- Feminine '-а' becomes '-у', and '-я' becomes '-ю': 'у субо́ту', 'у неді́лю', 'у п’я́тницю'.
- Masculine days are things, so they do not change: 'у понеді́лок', 'у четве́р'.
- 'Середа́' also moves its stress: 'у сере́ду'.

The euphony rules of the unit on stress choose between 'у' and 'в': 'в' after a vowel ('Що ти бу́деш роби́ти в субо́ту?'), 'у' after a consonant and at the start of a sentence ('Хо́чеш у парк у субо́ту?', 'У неді́лю я вдо́ма.'), and always 'у' before 'в' ('у вівто́рок').

The day itself is named in the nominative: 'Сього́дні п’я́тниця.', 'Today is Friday'; 'За́втра субо́та.', 'Tomorrow is Saturday'. 'На вихідни́х', on the weekend, is 'на' with the locative plural of 'вихідні́', met whole until the plural cases in A2.

The four seasons are nouns: 'зима́' and 'весна́' are feminine, 'лі́то' is neuter and 'о́сінь' is feminine. They name the season itself: 'Я люблю́ о́сінь.' To say that something happens in a season, Ukrainian uses an adverb, a single word that never changes, where English uses 'in' and the noun:

- 'зима́', winter: 'взи́мку', in winter
- 'весна́', spring: 'навесні́', in spring
- 'лі́то', summer: 'влі́тку', in summer
- 'о́сінь', autumn: 'восени́', in autumn

Each of these adverbs began as 'в' or 'на' joined to a form of the season's noun, but today each is one word, and none of them is a case form of the noun in the sentence. 'Взи́мку' and 'влі́тку' follow the rule of 'вдо́ма' and 'удо́ма': after a consonant and at the start of a sentence they begin with 'у' ('Тара́с узи́мку в Кана́ді.'). 'Навесні́' and 'восени́' have only one form.

examples.source: Taras is in Canada in winter.
The weather in Kyiv is nice in spring.

grammar.title: Weather: 'те́пло', 'хо́лодно' and 'Іде́ дощ.'
grammar.explanation:
English needs a subject in every sentence, so it says 'it is cold' and 'it is raining' with an 'it' that refers to nothing. Ukrainian talks about the weather with two other structures, and neither has a word for 'it'.

The first uses a predicative word. A predicative word is the whole predicate of a sentence with no grammatical subject, as 'мо́жна' is in the unit on food and drink. 'Те́пло' and 'хо́лодно' are predicative words: 'Сього́дні хо́лодно.' is literally 'today cold'. Since there is no subject, they have nothing to agree with and never change. They end in '-о' like many adverbs, but they are not adverbs here, because they do not describe a verb: they are the predicate. They can be made stronger with 'ду́же' and tied to a place: 'У Кана́ді ду́же хо́лодно.', 'Там те́пло.' In the future 'бу́де' joins them: 'За́втра бу́де те́пло.'

The second names the weather as the subject of a verb. Rain and snow 'go', with the verb 'іти́' of the unit on going places: 'Іде́ дощ.', 'it is raining', literally 'goes rain'; 'Іде́ сніг.', 'it is snowing'. After a vowel 'іде́' becomes 'йде': 'Сього́дні йде дощ.' The noun usually comes after the verb, because it is the new information. For the future, Ukrainian usually makes the noun the subject of 'бу́де': 'За́втра бу́де дощ.', 'it will rain tomorrow', literally 'tomorrow will-be rain'.

The sun shines with 'сві́тити', to shine, a verb of the second conjugation like 'говори́ти': 'Сві́тить со́нце.', 'the sun is shining', literally 'shines sun'.

To ask about the weather, use 'яки́й' in the feminine, because 'пого́да' is a feminine noun: 'Яка́ сього́дні пого́да?', 'What is the weather like today?'. 'Пого́да га́рна.' says that it is nice.

rows: What is the weather like today?

examples.source: It is very cold in Canada in winter.

culture.title: The week, the weekend and four seasons
culture.text:
The Ukrainian week begins on Monday, and calendars print Monday in the first column. The days are written with a small letter, like the words for nationalities, and most of their names say where the day falls in the week:

- 'неді́ля', Sunday, comes from 'не' and an old verb meaning 'to do' or 'to work': the day when no one works.
- 'понеді́лок', Monday, is the day after 'неді́ля'.
- 'вівто́рок', Tuesday, comes from an old word for 'second'.
- 'середа́', Wednesday, is the middle of the week; 'сере́дній', middle, has the same root.
- 'четве́р', Thursday, is the fourth day, and 'п’я́тниця', Friday, the fifth, from the roots of 'чоти́ри' and 'п’ять'.
- 'субо́та', Saturday, comes through Greek from the Hebrew word 'shabbat', the day of rest.

For office workers and schoolchildren, 'вихідні́' are Saturday and Sunday. Shops, markets, cafés and museums are usually open on both days, so many people who work in them have their days off during the week. On a free weekend, city people walk in the parks, meet friends in cafés, or visit relatives in the countryside, where many families keep a vegetable garden.

Ukraine has four distinct seasons. Winter brings frost and snow to most of the country: in Kyiv a January day is often a few degrees below freezing, and the Carpathian Mountains in the west are snowy enough for skiing. The south, along the Black Sea, is milder. Spring arrives in March and April, summer is warm to hot, with July days of 25 degrees or more, and autumn is often rainy. Temperatures are given in degrees Celsius, on which water freezes at zero.

A spell of warm, sunny days in early autumn is called 'ба́бине лі́то', literally 'grandmother's summer'. It is a favorite time for walks, when the chestnut trees of Kyiv turn yellow.

exercises.prompt: Match each day with its English name
Match each word with its English meaning

choices: On Sunday it will rain.
On Saturday it will rain.
On Saturday it will snow.

exercises.prompt: Why is there an apostrophe in 'п’я́тниця'?
choices: It keeps the 'п' hard and the [j] of 'я' sounded: [pj]
It marks the stressed syllable
It shows that the 'п' is soft
exercises.explanation: After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м', 'ф' and 'р', the apostrophe before 'я', 'ю', 'є' or 'ї' keeps the consonant hard and the [j] sounded. 'П’я́тниця' begins like 'п’ять', five.

exercises.prompt: How is the 'щ' at the end of 'дощ' said?
choices: [ʃ] alone, as in 'shoe'
[ʒ], as in 'measure'
[ʃt͡ʃ], as in 'fresh cheese', with both sounds in full
exercises.explanation: 'Щ' always writes the two sounds [ʃt͡ʃ], also at the end of a word, as in 'борщ'.

exercises.prompt: What tells 'те́пло', it is warm, from 'тепло́', warmth?
choices: The last letter
Only the stress
A soft 'л' in one of them
exercises.explanation: The two words have the same letters. 'Те́пло' is stressed on the first syllable and is a predicative word; 'тепло́' is stressed on the last and is a neuter noun. In ordinary text the sentence shows which one is meant.

choices: In autumn it often rains.
In spring it often rains.
In autumn it often snows.

exercises.explanation: The future of an imperfective verb is a form of 'бу́ти' plus the infinitive; the form for 'я' is 'бу́ду'.
Only 'бу́ти' changes for the person, and its form for 'ми' is 'бу́демо'; the infinitive 'працюва́ти' stays as it is.
A sentence with 'хо́лодно' has no subject, so 'бу́ти' takes the form of 'він', 'вона́', 'воно́': 'бу́де'.
A day takes 'у' or 'в' with the accusative. 'Середа́' is feminine, so '-а' becomes '-у', and the stress moves: 'сере́ду'.

exercises.hint_source: We relax at the lake in summer.
exercises.explanation: 'In summer' is the adverb 'влі́тку'. After a vowel it begins with 'в'; after a consonant it would be 'улі́тку'.
Rain 'goes' in Ukrainian: 'Іде́ дощ.' After the consonant at the end of 'за́раз', the form 'іде́' is the one euphony prefers.

exercises.audio_target: Що ти бу́деш роби́ти в неді́лю?
choices: Where will you be on Sunday?
What will you do on Monday?
What will you do on Sunday?

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'It will be warm tomorrow'?
choices: За́втра бу́де хо́лодно.
За́втра бу́де те́пло.
Сього́дні те́пло.
exercises.explanation: 'Бу́де' with 'те́пло' makes the future of a sentence with no subject. 'За́втра бу́де хо́лодно.' means 'It will be cold tomorrow', and 'Сього́дні те́пло.' means 'It is warm today'.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'вівто́рок' always take 'у', even after a vowel?
choices: 'Вівто́рок' is masculine
'В' is used only with feminine days
'У' always comes before a word that begins with 'в'
exercises.explanation: The euphony rule puts 'у' before 'в', 'ф', 'льв', 'св', 'тв' and 'хв' whatever comes before it.

choices: A predicative word: the whole predicate of a sentence with no grammatical subject
An adverb that describes 'сього́дні'
A form of the verb 'бу́ти'
exercises.explanation: 'Хо́лодно' is the predicate, and the sentence has no subject, so it has nothing to agree with and never changes. It is not an adverb here, because it describes no verb.

exercises.prompt: In 'Іде́ дощ.', what is the subject?
choices: There is none, as in 'Сього́дні хо́лодно.'
'Дощ': the rain is what 'goes'
A hidden word for 'it'
exercises.explanation: 'Дощ' is the subject and 'іде́' agrees with it. It comes after the verb because it is the new information.

exercises.prompt: Why can 'бу́ду' go with 'чита́ти' but never with 'прочита́ти'?
choices: 'Прочита́ти' is a verb of the second conjugation
'Прочита́ти' has no infinitive
'Бу́ду' makes the future of imperfective verbs only, and 'прочита́ти' is perfective
exercises.explanation: A perfective verb has a future of its own, which comes in A2. 'Бу́ду' plus an infinitive is the future of imperfective verbs such as 'чита́ти'.

exercises.prompt: Taras asks his sister 'Хо́чеш у парк у субо́ту?' What does he mean?
choices: Are you in the park on Saturday?
Do you want to go to the park on Saturday?
Do you like the park on Saturdays?
exercises.explanation: 'Хоті́ти' with a direction, 'у' plus the accusative 'парк', needs no verb of going. 'In the park' would be the locative 'у па́рку'.

exercises.prompt: Olena answers 'Ні, у субо́ту я працю́ю.' Why is 'працю́ю' in the present?
choices: A fixed plan with a time word can be in the present, as in English 'I'm working on Saturday'
'Працюва́ти' has no future
Ukrainian has no way to say 'will work'
exercises.explanation: 'Я бу́ду працюва́ти.' is also correct. The present with 'у субо́ту' presents the work as already arranged.

exercises.prompt: In class, Sam says 'Ні, я бу́ду тут, у Ки́єві.' What does he say?
choices: No, I am here, in Kyiv.
No, I was here, in Kyiv.
No, I will be here, in Kyiv.
exercises.explanation: 'Бу́ду' on its own is the future of 'бу́ти': 'I will be'. The present would have no verb: 'Я тут.'

exercises.hint_source: I will be at home on Sunday.

exercises.prompt_source: Where will you be on Sunday?
Will you be at home on Friday?
It will be warm on Thursday.
exercises.explanation: 'Четве́р' is a masculine thing, so the accusative after 'у' is unchanged, and the subjectless 'те́пло' takes 'бу́де'.
The future is 'бу́ду' plus the infinitive 'чита́ти', and the day is 'у неді́лю', or 'в неді́лю' after a vowel.

exercises.prompt_source: On Saturday we will be in the park.
answers: У субо́ту ми бу́демо в па́рку.
Ми бу́демо в па́рку в субо́ту.
Ми в субо́ту бу́демо в па́рку.
Ми бу́демо в субо́ту в па́рку.
exercises.explanation: 'Бу́демо' alone is 'we will be', and 'у па́рку' is the locative of place.

exercises.prompt_source: Do you want to go to the park on Sunday? (to a friend)
answers: Ти хо́чеш у парк у неді́лю?
Ти хо́чеш у неді́лю в парк?
У неді́лю ти хо́чеш у парк?
exercises.explanation: 'Хоті́ти' with 'у' plus the accusative needs no verb of going, and a friend is 'ти': 'хо́чеш'.
